articles.headline: Running LLMs in the Browser with Three.js
articles.blurb: Three-LLM runs GPT-2, SmolLM2, Qwen, and Phi models locally in the browser by turning their inference graphs into Three.js TSL compute shaders on WebGPU. The project was created to see how far the general computer capabilities of Three.js and WebGPU can be pushed, and to see what today's small language models can do when they run in a browser. Three.js is known as a rendering library, but its WebGPU renderer also exposes storage buffers, compute dispatches, workgroup memory, atomics, and GPU readback. Large language models put all of those capabilities to work as they need hundreds of ordered compute dispatches, large matrix-vector products, reductions, persistent attention or recurrent state, and a tight loop between the GPU and JavaScript as each new token appears.

The feature works for queue consumers and batch processors but requires at least one object or external metric, since CPU and memory metrics disappear once no pods are running. The approach lets dozens of dependent services keep calling the old cluster-internal DNS name while traffic silently routes to the new deployment, with no code changes required from other teams. A temporary policy exception handled the ingress side, allowing both the old and new ingress rules to coexist briefly while traffic was confirmed on the new deployment before the old one was removed.

articles.headline: Metal3 meets KubeVirtBMC: Provisioning KubeVirt VMs like bare metal
articles.blurb: KubeVirtBMC can be paired with Metal3, a CNCF incubating project, to provision KubeVirt virtual machines as if they were physical bare-metal servers. Metal3 uses OpenStack Ironic under the hood to handle hardware inspection, boot device control, and OS image writing via standard IPMI or Redfish interfaces. KubeVirtBMC creates virtual BMC endpoints for KubeVirt VMs, so Metal3 has no way to distinguish them from real hardware. This post walks through a full end-to-end setup that configures Redfish virtual media boot without PXE or DHCP and provisions a VM with a live ISO image.

articles.headline: How we could save petabytes of cache storage with Zstandard and Pingora
articles.blurb: Cloudflare has prototyped a system called Cache Transcoding that compresses eligible cached assets using the Zstandard algorithm before writing them to disk, shrinking those assets to roughly one-third of their original size on average. The system targets compressible text content like HTML, JSON, CSS, and JavaScript, which made up 67.3% of requests in Cloudflare's traffic sample but arrived uncompressed about 71% of the time. Encoding happens once when an asset enters the cache, while the CPU cost of decoding is paid on every serve at approximately 1.56 nanoseconds per byte. In testing across 10 cache servers with more than a million requests, the architecture stayed within its CPU budget at zstd level 3 with a 4 kibibyte minimum object size.
